source_document.body:
Khorfakkan
By Angelo Mathais India correspondent
17 November 2026
Apart from the lingering pressure of ocean freight rates that remain stubbornly elevated, India-Middle East shippers are facing various extra cost shocks, due to shifting carriers’ cargo handling policies and landside supply chain hurdles in the conflict region.
According to industry sources, fresh booking curbs imposed by mainline operators like Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd have further constrained capacity options for India’s cargo flows to the Persian Gulf.
With available vessel space from JNPA (Nhava Sheva) and Mundra to Khor Fakkan and Fujairah in the UAE, and Sohar in Oman, becoming tighter and more erratic, rates for these “lifeline” port pairs have risen from the levels seen last month, data suggests.
Spot rates offered by CMA CGM for JNPA to Khor Fakkan are around $7,500 per 40ft, compared with $6,500 to $7,000 in the second half of October.
Among the mainliners, CMA CGM has most sailings from India to the Persian Gulf via its Bigex network, as the carrier expanded Red Sea operations in a strategic approach. NVOs had traditionally dominated India-Middle East trade through slot deals with the mainline carriers.
“We do not expect any sort of rate relief in the near term,” one forwarder source told The Loadstar . “With fewer sailings, active capacity providers have the room to adjust rates dynamically.”
Rates ex-India to the other Gulf ports of discharge have also climbed month on month because of the supply-side issues, sources said.
CMA CGM’s spot rates for a 40ft booking from JNPA to Sohar are around $6,500, nearly double what the carrier was quoting at the end of September.
And the Gulf trade pain for shippers goes beyond soaring ocean rates. Hefty carrier charges linked to empty container drop-off at the destination are another significant cost. For example, Maersk is now charging as much as $1,200 per 40ft container for returns to the Sajaa dry port in the UAE, its designated yard for imports via Khor Fakkan. Sajaa, operated by Gulftainer, is roughly 90km from Khor Fakkan.
Maersk warned customers this week: “Vessel congestion and limited berthing availability at Khor Fakkan, together with high yard utilisation, road congestion and extended truck waiting times, are delaying cargo clearance.
“These conditions may affect import and export movements, including bonded transport to and from Ajman, Jebel Ali and other destinations.”
Similarly, Hapag-Lloyd, in a fresh Middle East operational update, has asked customers to confirm their preferred customs clearance or delivery location for UAE-bound imports by today, pushing them to pick up containers directly from the Sajaa depot, but also permitting collection at Khorfakkan, subject to requirements.
Customers who provide no instructions will have their cargo routed through Sajaa. The carrier said Sajaa offered 12 days of terminal free time and lower destination land freight charges.
UAE importers failing to notify the delivery instructions may run the risk of delayed customs clearance and additional storage/demurrage charges, in addition to container transfers imposed by Khor Fakkan terminal operators, sources said.
